perfil_profesional: Su intereses de investigación se centran en entender cómo los animales adquieren, almacenan, procesan y utilizan información para tomar decisiones, y las consecuencias de la toma de decisiones para el individuo y para el grupo. Esta aproximación se enmarca en la llamada Ecología cognitiva, la cual integra herramientas y constructos teóricos de distintas ramas como la neurobiología, las ciencias cognitivas, la ecología conductual y la fisiología. Como modelo utiliza principalmente insectos, en especial abejas, hormigas y mariposas.

proyectos: Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo Brain correlates of social complexity in ants Inicio: Mayo 2006 Fin: Agosto 2006 Duración 0 Resumen Several changes at individual and group levels- have accompanied the emergence and evolution of social complexity. The nervous system, for instance, as the physical substrate of behavior presumably changed to allow individuals acquire and manipulate new information related with social life. Such relationships between brain and social life have been previously evaluated in vertebrates. However, highly complex societies also occur in some invertebrate taxa, in which factors driving social evolution are different. Those differences might be reflected in traits describing social complexity. In insects, for instance, evolution of social complexity involves two main factors: specialization of a worker caste and evolution of communication systems. The link between such factors of insect social complexity and brain structures has not been previously evaluated. In this project, I propose to test the hypothesis that different levels of social complexity in insects go along with morphological changes in brain structures. I will compare representative species of eight genera of fungus-growing ants (Hymenoptera: Attini) for which variation in social complexity and phylogenetic relations among the genera are well established. For brain comparisons, I will measure volumes of brain areas involving acquisition, processing and storing of different kinds of information. I predict an increase in the volume of particular areas as consequence of behavioral specialization (division of labor), and the increase on complexity of communication systems. Additionally, as communication in ants involves mainly chemical pheromones, I will analyze in more detail brain areas where chemical cues are represented. I predict an increase in the amount of the neural substrate devoted to chemical processing as the chemical communication becomes more complex.

Tipo de proyecto: Investigación, desarrollo e Innovación Desarrollo de composiciones y mecanismos para la protección cognitiva de polinizadores Inicio: Junio 2019 Duración Resumen La desaparición de las abejas es un problema global con impactos económicos y ecológicos. Un elemento crítico en la desaparición lo juegan los pesticidas, que pueden generar efectos subletales sobre el sistema cognitivo. Las estrategias desde la academia se han dirigido principalmente a la recopilación de evidencia que pueda ser utilizada para la elaboración de políticas de uso de pesticidas. Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo Correlations between brain anatomy and complex behavior in bumblebees Inicio: Enero 2005 Fin: Enero 2005 Duración 12 Resumen Insect societies are characterized by division of labor between specialized groups of individuals. Such specialization may depend on an individual's age or morphology. For example, honeybee foragers are older than nest workers ('nurses'), whereas in army ants soldiers are the largest individuals. Importantly, division of labor can be associated with cognitive specialization and brain development. For example, in honeybees, ants and wasps, a correlation exists between the tasks performed and the size of a specific brain structure, the so-called mushroom bodies (MB). MB underlie important behavioral functions such as learning and memory, which are more important for foragers than for nest worker: foragers rely on visual learning for navigation and the acquisition of spatial memories whereas nest workers ('nurses') do not rely on vision in their the dark environment. In several hymenoptera, such behavioral differences coincide with consistently larger visual MB-areas in foragers than in ¿nurses¿. We propose to analyze MB anatomy in bumblebees, which exhibit division of labor based mainly on body size. Larger bumblebees are more efficient foragers and better learners, and preliminary data indicate that they have bigger MBs. However, it is not known if foraging behavior or MB size also depend on the age of bumblebees, as it does in honey bees. We will analyze small, intermediate and large bumblebees (Bombus impatiens) from laboratory colonies. Newly emerged bees will be marked and measured in order to track the individual's age and behavioral repertoires. The bees' brains will then be dissected, fixed, stained and morphometrically examined.

Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo Cognitive and Neural Basis of Insect Sociality Inicio: Agosto 2007 Fin: Agosto 2009 Duración Resumen Several changes ¿at individual and group levels- have accompanied the emergence and evolution of social complexity. The nervous system, for instance, as the physical substrate of behavior presumably changed to allow individuals to acquire and manipulate new information related with social life. Such relationships between brain and social life have been previously evaluated in vertebrates. However, highly complex societies also occur in some invertebrate taxa, in which factors driving social evolution are different. Those differences might be reflected in traits describing social complexity. In insects, for instance, evolution of social complexity involves two main factors: specialization of a worker caste and evolution of communication systems. The link between such factors of insect social complexity and neural and cognitive features has not been previously evaluated. Here, I propose to test the hypothesis that high levels of behavioral specialization in social insects go along with changes in neural morphology and cognitive features. As workers specialize on particular tasks, their overall behavioral repertoire will be reduced whereas their ability to perform the particular task will be refined. I therefore predict that some brain areas that support the workers¿ particular tasks will exhibit an increase, whereas an overall decrease of the relative total brain volume would be expected. Moreover, I predict an increase in cognitive performance of individuals specialized for tasks involving more information processing (e.g. foraging).

Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo Interpretation of unimodal and multimodal information by bees Inicio: Octubre 2012 Fin: Diciembre 2014 Duración Resumen Many biological systems rely on the use of sensory multimodal rather than unimodal signals for communication. That multimodal displays entail high energetic costs but are very common in nature suggests that benefits surpass the costs. Also, that receivers of information have evolved to interpret such multimodal signals suggests benefits on their side. The goal of this project is to evaluate functional hypotheses suggesting that complex (multimodal) signals may enhance the acquisition, processing and retrieval of information. This project also aims to evaluate whether the animal model (namely the bumblebees) is able to interpret complex (multimodal) signals as unique configurations rather than simple sum of independent components.
